question: Will the UK increase the qualifying period for settlement to 10 years before May 2026?
summary: The objections identify credible downward risks: political turnover, regulatory complexity, and exemptions curbing universality of a 10-year path by May 2026.
Threshold analysis shows a 10-year baseline is plausible but not guaranteed; timing depends on legislation, regulatory changes, and the public consultation outcomes.
Official momentum toward a 10-year baseline remains strong (White Paper, public consultation), supporting a high likelihood despite caveats.
Net calibration: modest downward adjustment from the ensemble to reflect these downside risks, yielding a probability around 0.68.

justification.critique_assessment: Objections are valid and reveal real risks that could delay or limit a universal 10-year settlement; they justify a downward calibration, though they do not render the outcome implausible.
justification.adjustment: Adjusted downward from 0.76 to 0.68 to account for political, regulatory, and exemption-related risks; no physically implausible scenarios invoked. The adjustment reflects credible but not certain impediments to a universal 10-year path by May 2026.

forecasts.reference-class: UK immigration policy on settlement eligibility; 10-year baseline for most migrants as proposed in the 2025 White Paper 'Restoring Control over the Immigration System', with a time-adjustment model and exceptions.

sources.claim: White Paper published 12 May 2025 proposes a 10-year baseline qualifying period for settlement for most migrants, with a time-adjustment model; consultation open until 12 February 2026.

House of Commons Library briefing says the baseline qualifying period would be ten years for many migrants (with some groups qualifying sooner) and notes the public consultation until 12 February 2026.
Migration Observatory analysis indicates the scheme would set a 10-year baseline for most migrants, with longer waits for many groups; high earners could qualify after five years.
ILPA briefing on the White Paper discusses the proposals, including a 10-year baseline and a time-adjustment framework feeding into settlement rules.

The government proposes an earned settlement model with a default 10-year qualifying period for settlement, plus a time-adjustment framework across four pillars (character, integration, contribution, residence).
HC 836 (June 2025) documents the then-current rules, including cases where a 5-year qualifying period for settlement applied, against which reforms are being proposed.
House of Commons Library briefing (Nov 2025) states the baseline 10-year period with exemptions and notes a public consultation through February 2026.
Migration Observatory analysis summarizes a shift toward a 10-year baseline with exemptions and outlines how the earned settlement model might operate, with consultation closing in February 2026.
Long residence guidance confirms a 10-year continuous lawful presence requirement for settlement under the long-residence route.

The default qualifying period for settlement will be increased from five years to ten years under the earned settlement model; the consultation is open and will run until 12 February 2026; changes could be implemented once immigration rules are changed.

House of Commons Library briefing states the government’s plan is to raise the baseline qualifying period to 10 years, with changes potentially taking effect from April 2026, subject to the public consultation ending 12 February 2026.
The long residence route currently requires 10 years of continuous lawful residence for settlement.

synthesis: Policy signals point toward a 10-year settlement baseline, but real-world frictions—political risk, implementation complexity, and exemptions—introduce meaningful downside. The final probability is calibrated downward from the ensemble to reflect these credible obstacles, while still recognizing strong momentum.
